title: A study to investigate if Levodopa (a Parkinson’s medication) can help people with wet age-related macular degeneration
official: Levodopa (L-DOPA) for neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration (AMD): a randomised controlled trial (LAMDARCT)
summary:
Background and study aims 
Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) typically first affects people in their 50s or 60s, disrupting central vision and making everyday activities difficult. There are two forms of AMD, dry and wet. In wet AMD, new vessels grow into the retina (light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye) and destroy it. Vision can deteriorate quickly; therefore, timely intervention is critical.

Injections of medications into the eye can slow the progression to blindness in wet AMD. Multiple injections are often needed for years. Injections into the eye are uncomfortable, inconvenient and can have complications. Furthermore, injections into the eye are one of the most expensive treatments in the NHS.

This study is important as it looks at a way to reduce the number of injections into the eye while preserving sight. This is important for patients, carers, and the NHS. L-DOPA tablets are used for treating people with Parkinson’s disease and are an effective, safe treatment. Recent studies showed that those who take L-DOPA develop AMD at an older age. In addition, in another small study, those who had wet AMD and took L-DOPA needed fewer injections. 

A well-designed clinical trial is needed to confirm that L-DOPA can reduce the number of injections into the eye, maintain vision and be well tolerated.

Who can participate? 
Adult patients aged 50 years and older with newly diagnosed wet AMD. 

What does the study involve? 
Participants will receive either L-DOPA or placebo tablets for two years while receiving normal treatment. The number of injections needed to maintain vision after two years will be compared between the treatment groups. The study will also confirm if L-DOPA is well-tolerated and whether it is good value for money. It will compare the quality of life of participants and investigate how L-DOPA helps in maintaining vision. Eye imaging examinations will be used to study the retina further to confirm this.

Participants will need to take one capsule twice a day for the majority of the 2 years on the trial. For the final 4 weeks of treatment, the dose will be reduced gradually to avoid side effects. This will involve taking 1 capsule per day for 2 weeks, then 1 capsule on alternate days or 2 weeks before stopping the drug. The study visits require attending the clinic for five visits at baseline, 24, 48, 72 and 104 weeks. There will also be 2 safety phone calls with participants, to collect any adverse events within 1 week and at week 108 (4 weeks after stopping treatment). A short phone call at week 100 will also advise the participant on the gradual dose reduction prior to stopping treatment.

Participants will also be asked to report adverse events and tolerability outcomes as they happen, by contacting the site research team using contact details provided.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
The medication used in this trial is well established and has been generally well tolerated in people with Parkinson's disease. While participants may not experience a direct benefit from taking part, the information gained may help improve treatment and care for people with Parkinson's disease in the future.

Possible side effects when starting the medication include nausea, tiredness, and dizziness. These effects are usually mild and temporary and often improve within a few days. People who may be at higher risk from the medication, such as those who are pregnant or taking dopamine receptor agonists, will not be eligible to participate.

Participant safety will be monitored throughout the study. Participants will be contacted shortly after starting the medication to check for side effects and will undergo scheduled safety assessments, including blood tests and clinical evaluations, during study visits. Participants will also be provided with contact details for the study team should they have any concerns or experience any side effects during the trial.

Where is the study run from?  
Belfast Health and Social Care Trust, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
October 2026 to April 2030.

Who is funding the study? 
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), UK.

Who is the main contact?
Prof T Peto, t.peto@qub.ac.uk
criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	New diagnosis of wet AMD in the study eye
2.	≥50 years old
3.	Commenced treatment with anti-VEGF and still within the initial period of loading treatment (i.e. not completed loading doses)
Exclusion criteria:
1.	Patients who are taking dopamine receptor agonists or dopamine-blocking medication
2.	Diagnosis of Parkinson’s disease, restless leg syndrome, orthostatic hypotension or recognised movement disorder
3.	Confirmed narrow-angle glaucoma
4.	Uncontrolled chronic wide-angle glaucoma
5.	History of melanoma or suspicious skin lesion under evaluation
6.	Severe renal or hepatic impairment
7.	Conditions in which adrenergics are contraindicated e.g. hyperthyroidism, Cushing’s syndrome, severe cardiovascular disease
8.	History of MI with residual atrial nodal or ventricular arrythmias
9.	Severe pulmonary disease
10.	Uncontrolled Bronchial asthma 
11.	History of peptic ulcer disease (if active or recurrent)
12.	Current or history of severe or uncontrolled psychiatric disorders, including psychosis or psychotic disorders 
13.	Known or suspected pheochromocytoma
14.	Receiving three or more anti-hypertensive drugs 
15.	Receiving non-selective monoamine oxidase (MAO) inhibitors and selective MAO type A inhibitors (or received within the past 14 days)
16.	Known hypersensitivity or contraindications to the IMP
17.	Patients already receiving anti-VEGF injections for another eye condition
18.	Pregnancy, lactating, or, in the case of women of child-bearing potential, unwillingness to use medically approved contraception during treatment
19.	Male participants unwilling to use medically approved contraception during treatment
20.	Current participation in another Interventional clinical trial or participation in such a clinical trial within the last six months
21.	Unable to take the study medication *
22.	Unable to adhere to the trial protocol/schedule of assessments
23.	Unable to provide consent to be involved in the study
24.	Declined consent for participation
